key_insight: In this EHR study, AI-related interactions in psychosis were uncommon but appeared as a real clinical pattern, most often when AI seemed to reinforce or amplify distorted beliefs.
clinical_relevance: The findings suggest clinicians should be alert to AI use in patients with psychosis, especially during first episodes, because conversational AI may worsen delusional thinking in some cases.
method: Searched Vanderbilt University Medical Center EHRs from 12/1/2022 to 4/1/2026 for AI-related keywords.
Excluded records that were not AI-related or did not have psychosis as the primary diagnosis.
Three raters classified cases into Catalyst, Amplifier, Co-Author, or Object interaction types.
evidence_signal: Among 73 eligible patients, 28 were judged to have AI psychosis, with 60.7% of that group in a first psychotic episode and 64.3% rated as Amplifier cases.
watch_item: This is a single-center retrospective EHR analysis, so documentation quality and keyword-based case finding may miss or misclassify AI use and limit generalizability.
paper_title: Characterizing artificial intelligence (AI) psychosis in a large academic medical setting: evidence of the new clinical phenomenon and the vulnerability of those in early phases of psychosis
